...if I lie in any way. I know a certain man who is a master of many arts <note>original Greek: πολυτεχνότατον</note>, a scholar of Greek, Latin, mathematics, philosophy, and medicine <note>original Greek: καὶ ταῦτα βασιλικόν; meaning "and even of the royal kind"</note>. Now in his sixties, he has set aside all other things and for more than twenty years has tortured and racked himself over grammar. He believes he would be truly happy if he were permitted to live long enough to determine with certainty how the eight parts of speech ought to be distinguished, a task which no Greek or Latin scholar has yet been able to fully achieve. It is as if it were a matter to be settled by war if someone treats a conjunction as a word belonging to the category of adverbs. 

For this reason, since there are as many grammars as there are grammarians—or rather more, since my friend Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius, the famous Venetian printer and scholar</note> has published his own grammar more than five times—this man never overlooks any book, no matter how barbarously or tediously written. He examines and scrutinizes them all, envying anyone else who attempts anything in this field, however foolishly. He lives in wretched fear that someone might snatch away this glory or that his many years of labor might be lost. Would you prefer to call this insanity or Folly? <summary>Folly describes a multi-talented scholar who has wasted twenty years obsessing over the minutiae of grammar and the eight parts of speech. She highlights the absurdity of such academic pedantry and the vanity of grammarians like Aldus Manutius.</summary>
<keywords>Erasmus, Folly, grammar, pedantry, Aldus Manutius, scholarship, academic vanity, parts of speech</keywords>
